stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

Match each part of the label to what it tells you.
explanation: Barolo is the DOCG designation; Bussia is the vineyard the grapes came from (the course's own example, Barolo Bussia); 2018 is the harvest year; Riserva means longer maturation in barrel than usual. There is no commercial name on this label, and Nebbiolo is implied by the designation rather than printed.

stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

Which element is the **designation** of the wine?
explanation: The designation identifies the wine by production area together with its winemaking rules and grape — here Barolo DOCG. Bussia is a vineyard name added after it, and Riserva is an ageing term.

stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

What does **Bussia** tell you?
choices: the vineyard that grew the grapes
the estate that bottled the wine
the village where the cellar stands today
the grape variety in the bottle
explanation: In Italy a producer may add the vineyard after the designation: in *Barolo Bussia*, Barolo is the DOCG and Bussia is the vineyard.

stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

What does **Riserva** promise?
choices: a longer maturation in barrel than usual
a higher alcohol than the minimum allowed
a blend made only from one good harvest
grapes from the historic core of the zone
explanation: Riserva (Reserve) means longer ageing in cask or barrel than the designation requires. Higher alcohol is *Superiore*; the historic core is *Classico*; a single good year is *Millésime/Millesimato*.

stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

**2018** is the year the grapes were harvested. What is that called on a label?
explanation: The vintage is the year of harvesting — item 3 of the seven main details on a label.

stem:
A label reads, top to bottom: **Cantina Belvedere** · **BAROLO** · Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita · **Bussia** · **Riserva** · **2018** · 14.5% vol · 750 ml · Bottled by Cantina Belvedere, Piemonte.

Which grape is this wine made from?
explanation: Barolo DOCG (and Barbaresco DOCG) in Piemonte are made from Nebbiolo — highly tannic, long-lived, complex.

stem:
A label reads: **Château Margaux** · Premier Grand Cru Classé · **MARGAUX** · Appellation Margaux Contrôlée · **2015** · 13.5% vol · 750 ml.

The producer and the designation share a name here. Which reading is right?
choices: Margaux AOC is the producer; Château Margaux is the designation
Château Margaux is the designation; Margaux is the commercial name
Château Margaux is the producer; Margaux AOC is the designation
Château Margaux is the vineyard; Margaux is the bottling agency
explanation: The course's own example: Producer Château Margaux, Designation Margaux AOC, Region Médoc. A Bordeaux château name is the producer; the *Appellation … Contrôlée* line is the designation.

stem:
A label reads: **Château Margaux** · Premier Grand Cru Classé · **MARGAUX** · Appellation Margaux Contrôlée · **2015** · 13.5% vol · 750 ml.

What is **Premier Grand Cru Classé**?
choices: a fantasy name chosen by the producer
the designation the wine is sold under
the name of the single vineyard plot the grapes grew in
a ranking of the producer inside the designation
explanation: Within one French designation there can be a sub-classification of producers, such as Premier Grand Cru Classé. It ranks the producer; the designation is still Margaux AOC.

stem:
A label reads: **Château Margaux** · Premier Grand Cru Classé · **MARGAUX** · Appellation Margaux Contrôlée · **2015** · 13.5% vol · 750 ml.

Which grape leads this left-bank wine?
explanation: Margaux is on the left bank (Médoc), the Cabernet Sauvignon zone; its clay gives a softer, 'feminine' Cabernet. Merlot leads on the right bank (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol).

stem:
A label reads: **Fattoria del Colle** · **Il Falco** · Toscana · Indicazione Geografica Tipica · **2019** · Cabernet Sauvignon – Sangiovese · 14% vol · 750 ml.

What is **Il Falco**?
choices: the vineyard the grapes grew in
explanation: Beyond the designation, a producer may add a commercial or 'fantasy' name. Fattoria del Colle is the producer, and the designation is Toscana IGT.

stem:
A label reads: **Fattoria del Colle** · **Il Falco** · Toscana · Indicazione Geografica Tipica · **2019** · Cabernet Sauvignon – Sangiovese · 14% vol · 750 ml.

What does **Indicazione Geografica Tipica** tell you about this wine?
choices: it is the largest and most medium-quality class
it is made to no production specification at all
it holds Italy's highest designation with a quality guarantee
it is a quality wine made outside DOC or DOCG rules
explanation: IGT is usually a quality wine that does not follow DOC/DOCG regulations — the home of many Super Tuscans. DOCG is the highest, DOC the largest, VdT has no specification.

stem:
A label reads: **Fattoria del Colle** · **Il Falco** · Toscana · Indicazione Geografica Tipica · **2019** · Cabernet Sauvignon – Sangiovese · 14% vol · 750 ml.

True or false: because it is not DOC or DOCG, this must be a low-quality wine.
explanation: IGT (and IGP/VDQS-type classes) exist precisely for producers who make high-quality wine outside the designation rules — Tignanello and Solaia are Rosso IGT.

stem:
A label reads: **Maison Dubois** · **CHAMPAGNE** · Blanc de Blancs · Brut · Millésime 2016 · 12% vol · 750 ml.

What does **Blanc de Blancs** tell you?
choices: it is made from Pinot Noir alone
it is a blend of all three grapes
it is made from Chardonnay alone
it is made from Pinot Meunier alone
explanation: Blanc de Blancs is sparkling wine from Chardonnay only — the only grape used in Blanc de Blancs Champagne. From Pinot Noir only, it is Blanc de Noirs.

stem:
A label reads: **Maison Dubois** · **CHAMPAGNE** · Blanc de Blancs · Brut · Millésime 2016 · 12% vol · 750 ml.

What does **Millésime 2016** promise?
choices: the house was granted Grand Cru status in 2016
the wine aged on its yeast for at least 2016 days
the bottle is number 2016 of a limited run
over 85% of the cuvée comes from the 2016 harvest
explanation: If more than 85% of the base cuvée comes from one good production year, the sparkling wine is called Millésime (vintage).

stem:
A label reads: **Maison Dubois** · **CHAMPAGNE** · Blanc de Blancs · Brut · Millésime 2016 · 12% vol · 750 ml.

**Brut** places the residual sugar in which band?
explanation: Dosage scale, driest to sweetest: Pas dosé <1, Brut nature <3, Extra brut <6, Brut <15, Extra dry 12–20, Sec 18–35, Demi-sec 33–50, Doux >50 g/L.

stem: Match each sparkling-wine dosage term to its residual sugar.
explanation: Pas dosé <1, Brut nature <3, Extra brut <6, Brut <15, Extra dry 12–20, Sec 18–35, Demi-sec 33–50, Doux >50. Note the trap: Extra dry is *sweeter* than Brut.

stem: On the sparkling-wine dosage scale, Extra dry is sweeter than Brut.
explanation: Counter-intuitive but on the slide: Brut <15 g/L, Extra dry 12–20 g/L.

stem: On the sparkling-wine dosage scale, Demi-sec is drier than Extra brut.
explanation: Demi-sec is 33–50 g/L; Extra brut is under 6 g/L. Only Doux (>50) is sweeter than Demi-sec.

stem: Which of these is one of the seven main details the course lists for a wine label?
choices: the soil type of the vineyard
explanation: The seven: producer logo, designation, vintage, bottling agency and producer, alcohol (% vol), volume, and bottling number/sequence. Descriptions, serving temperature and food may be added, but are extras.

stem: How is alcohol content shown on a wine label?
explanation: Alcohol content is given in percent by volume (% vol) — one of the seven main details.

stem: The course uses a French word for the wine label. What is it?
explanation: Étiquette — the Italian equivalent is *etichetta*. Don't confuse it with serving etiquette.

stem: What does an Italian producer call the wine label?
explanation: Etichetta. The French is étiquette.

stem: A designation identifies a wine by its area of production together with…
choices: its producer's name and the agency that bottled it
its alcohol content and bottle volume
its vintage and its bottling sequence
its winemaking technique and grape varietal
explanation: Designation = production area + winemaking technique + grape varietal. Producer, alcohol, volume and vintage are separate details on the label.

stem: On an Italian label, *Superiore* means the wine reached a higher alcohol than its designation requires.
explanation: Superiore = at least 0.5% more alcohol than the stated minimum. Longer barrel ageing is *Riserva*.

stem: On an Italian label, *Superiore* means the wine spent longer in barrel than its designation requires.
explanation: That is Riserva. Superiore is about alcohol: at least 0.5% above the designation's minimum.

stem: *Classico* is added to designations with a long history of production, such as Chianti Classico and Soave Classico.
explanation: Classico marks the historic production zone of a designation.

stem: By how much must an Italian *Superiore* exceed its designation's minimum alcohol?
explanation: Superiore needs a minimum of 0.5% more alcohol than stated in the designation.

stem: Match each label term to its meaning.
explanation: Riserva = longer ageing in cask; Superiore = ≥0.5% more alcohol; Classico = the historic heart of the zone; Millésime = >85% of the cuvée from one good year.

stem: A label reads **Chianti Classico DOCG · Riserva · 2019**. What does Riserva require here?
explanation: Chianti Classico: min 12% alcohol. Riserva: min 24 months' maturation (incl. 3 months' bottle fining) and 12.5% alcohol.

stem: Which Chianti Classico category, introduced in 2014, is made only from the winery's own grapes under stricter rules? (two words)
explanation: Chianti Classico Gran Selezione (2014): exclusively the estate's own grapes, stricter than regular Chianti Classico.

stem: A label reads **Marsala Superiore Riserva**. How long has it aged?
explanation: Marsala ageing: Fine 1 yr, Superiore 2, Superiore Riserva 4, Vergine/Soleras 5, Stravecchio/Riserva 10.

stem: Match each classification to its country and level.
explanation: France: AOC > Vin de Pays > Vin de France. Italy: DOCG > DOC > IGT > VdT (Vino da Tavola).

stem: Which Italian classification is the *largest* in the country, usually for medium-quality wine?
explanation: DOC is the largest designation, usually medium quality but sometimes as good as DOCG. DOCG adds a quality guarantee on top of strict control.

stem: DOCG adds a guarantee of quality on top of the strict production control that DOC already has.
explanation: Controllata e *Garantita*: controlled and guaranteed.

stem: Vin de Pays is the strictest French category, above AOC.
explanation: AOC is the highest and strictest; Vin de Pays is less regulated; Vin de France is the base level.

stem: On a Bourgogne label, which of these names alone (no village) marks a **Grand cru**?
explanation: Grand cru wines carry the Grand cru name without a village (Corton, Montrachet). Premier cru is labelled Premier cru + village; Bourgogne Aligoté and Mâcon-Villages are regional appellations.

stem: A Bourgogne Premier cru is labelled with the village name followed by Premier cru.
explanation: Premier cru = village name + Premier cru (about 12% of production). Grand cru carries no village name.

stem: A label reads **Bourgogne Aligoté**. What kind of appellation is it?
choices: a Grand cru naming the vineyard
a Premier cru naming the climat
a regional appellation naming the grape
a village appellation naming the commune
explanation: Regional appellations can be AOC Bourgogne, AOC + sub-zone (Mâcon-Villages) or AOC + grape (Bourgogne Aligoté).

stem: Bourgogne ranks its wines by terroir in four levels. Which order runs from highest to lowest?
choices: Grand cru › Village › Premier cru › Regional
Premier cru › Grand cru › Village › Regional
Grand cru › Premier cru › Village › Regional
Premier cru › Village › Grand cru › Regional
explanation: Grand cru (best terroir, ~2%) › Premier cru (~12%) › Village appellation › Regional appellation.

stem: A label reads *Alsace · Riesling · Vendange Tardive*. Vendange Tardive is an Alsace sweet-wine style.
explanation: Vendange Tardive and Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN) are Alsace's important sweet styles.

stem: Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC is the only Italian designation tied to one specific wine and producer.
explanation: Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC (Tenuta San Guido) — the one designation tied to a single wine name and producer.

stem: On an Italian label, *Classico* means the wine was aged in barrel for longer than usual.
explanation: Classico marks a designation's historic production zone (Chianti Classico, Soave Classico). Longer ageing is Riserva.

stem: A Bourgogne Grand cru label shows the village name followed by the words Grand cru.
explanation: Grand cru wines carry the Grand cru name *without* a village (Corton, Montrachet). Village + Premier cru is the Premier cru format.

stem: A Champagne labelled Blanc de Blancs may include Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier in its blend.
explanation: Blanc de Blancs is Chardonnay only.
